part.text:
Lowering corporate taxes doesn't reliably create jobs because:

**Companies prioritize returns, not tax rates.** Investment decisions depend on consumer demand, regulations, and expected profitability—not marginal tax savings. When demand is weak, lower taxes don't spur hiring.

**Benefits flow to shareholders, not workers.** Most tax savings go to stock buybacks (up 84% of gains 2018-2019 post-cut) and executive compensation, per Federal Reserve data. Only ~25% might trickle to wages or investment.

**No historical evidence.** The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act produced a brief Hiring bump that faded within two years. Long-term employment fell below pre-cut trends as companies cut jobs while reporting record profits.

**Jobs follow demand, not supply-side promises.** Workers are hired when consumers have purchasing power. Lower taxes on corporations—the wealthiest entity—doesn't put money in workers' pockets the way raising the minimum wage or expanding earned-income credits would.

In short: tax cuts shift wealth upward but don't create employment. Jobs require workers with spending power and businesses with confidence that enough people will buy their products to turn a profit.
